I've been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when they first introduced the T-Mobile ONE plan. Throughout my time with them, I've always had a military discount, but even with that, T-Mobile's price hikes had pushed my monthly bill up to $113. I decided I'd had enough and started looking for cheaper alternatives. On top of that, with this year's Apple iPhone 18 Pro costing at least $100 more, I figured that if I was going to get a new phone anyway, reducing my monthly bill might help offset the cost. So I started looking into MVNOs.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." Simply put, an MVNO is a wireless carrier that doesn't operate its own nationwide cellular network. They buy network access from one of the major carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon) and resell the service to their own customers. Think of them as middlemen for wireless service.

Switching to an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up the network you're already on. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's, and US Mobile lets you choose which of the three major networks you want to use. In this article, I'll focus on these three MVNOs because they're the ones I researched most thoroughly before leaving T-Mobile, but there are plenty of other options out there.

Simply put, an MVNO gives you another way to buy wireless service without going directly to the company that owns the network.

Why are MVNOs cheaper? And what are the "catches"?

If an MVNO uses the same cellular network as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can it charge so much less? The simple answer is that MVNOs don't have to shoulder all the costs of running a nationwide wireless carrier. They don't build or maintain their own networks, many operate primarily online without physical stores, and they have fewer employees. The savings are passed on to customers in the form of lower monthly fees.

MVNO plans tend to be simpler, without the "perks" and add-on deals that traditional big carriers often offer. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or other perks designed to keep you locked in. But the money you save by going with an MVNO, if you really want those "free" perks, still leaves you with extra cash to subscribe on your own.

This was certainly the case for me. I used T-Mobile's free MLB.TV subscription every season, but I never watch Netflix, so the "Netflix on Us" perk was completely useless to me. Even if I wanted both, I could pay for the subscriptions myself and still come out ahead after factoring in the savings from switching. At the end of the day, I primarily wanted a reliable and affordable wireless service, without T-Mobile bundling a bunch of extras I didn't need.

The so-called "catches" aren't about poorer service quality, but about buying less. What exactly you give up depends on which MVNO and which plan you choose. Video streaming might be limited to lower resolution, high-speed or premium data allowances may differ, and network priority may vary. I have extremely fast Wi-Fi at home and rarely go to concerts or stadiums where things get "congested," so network priority isn't that important for my daily use. But I travel internationally occasionally, so international data is an important consideration. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others charge extra, or offer more limited coverage outside the US.

There are also some less obvious differences, especially when buying a new iPhone. If you choose an MVNO as your carrier, Apple Card installment payments and the iPhone Upgrade Program aren't available. If you want to use either of those options, you're limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. Practically speaking, if you buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you generally have to pay it all at once. Big carriers can also offer substantial trade-in deals and other promotions that generally aren't available through MVNOs. Apple Watch support isn't available with all MVNOs either, so if you use a cellular Apple Watch, that's something to keep in mind.

Finally, most MVNOs rely on phone and online support more than face-to-face staff at physical stores. I consider myself fairly tech-savvy, and I don't want to wait in line at a store just to get help. And in my experience, store salespeople end up calling the same phone number to wait for the same people anyway, so I can just as easily do it from home. This isn't a big deal to me.

Most importantly, none of these are inherent limitations of MVNOs. It depends on the carrier and plan, so it's worth looking carefully at exactly what you're getting before you switch.

Three MVNOs Worth Considering

After I decided to leave T-Mobile, I started looking for alternatives. Verizon's and AT&T's postpaid plans were even more expensive than what I was already paying, so the other two big carriers were off the table for me. I ultimately narrowed my search to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something that appealed to me, and all of them would allow me to significantly reduce my monthly bill without forcing me to give up using a major carrier's network.

US Mobile is arguably the most flexible of the three, and it's the carrier I ultimately chose after leaving T-Mobile. That doesn't mean it's necessarily the best fit for you, or necessarily the best MVNO of the three. It's purely the choice that suited me best.

US Mobile wasn't actually my first choice. I'd never even heard of the company before I started researching MVNOs. But the more I looked at what it offered, the more it stood out. Here's why: US Mobile offers service on all three major US networks, letting customers choose the network that suits them best. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on that lets you activate two networks on the same iPhone at the same time, without needing an additional phone number. Both networks are tied to the same line, and your iPhone can use whichever signal is better for calls and data. That means if T-Mobile's network works great at your workplace but Verizon's is better at home, you can use both without carrying two phones or managing two different numbers. US Mobile charges extra for this, and I don't personally need the feature, but it's a pretty unique option to have.

I recently moved, and I was curious how Verizon's coverage compared to T-Mobile's near my new home, so I decided to test both networks myself. I set my wife's iPhone to US Mobile's Light Speed network (which is T-Mobile), and my iPhone on Warp (which is Verizon), so we could compare coverage firsthand. We found that Verizon was noticeably better in our area, so switching to US Mobile was truly a win-win: better coverage and a much lower monthly bill.

Mint Mobile was originally my top choice because it's owned by T-Mobile, meaning I could stay on the same network I'm familiar with, but at a much lower price. What I didn't like was that it doesn't include international data. My wife and I love taking cruises, and travel is a regular part of our lives, so having cellular data outside the US is important to us. Mint does offer international data, but it costs extra, and it would quickly eat into some of the savings. I also didn't like that taxes and fees were billed separately.

Visible is similarly simple, but it only uses Verizon's network. My biggest hesitation with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. I'd been a T-Mobile customer for nearly a decade, so I knew exactly how T-Mobile's network performed, but I had no idea about Verizon's coverage. That was really the only thing that stopped me from choosing Visible over US Mobile, because US Mobile let me try Verizon's network while still having T-Mobile and AT&T as options if Verizon didn't work out. Visible's top-tier unlimited plan also includes a free cellular Apple Watch plan, which was appealing. (US Mobile's top-tier plan on its Warp (Verizon) network offers the same perk.)

What You Need to Switch

Switching to an MVNO was even simpler than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and transferring both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile took about ten minutes. I didn't even have to get off the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, though I'm focusing on iPhone here), and some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your existing phone number, don't cancel your old service before the number transfer goes through.

Here's what you'll need to switch:

  • Account number from your current carrier
  • Transfer PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I prepaid for a year of US Mobile's unlimited plan for both lines to prepare for the switch. My wife doesn't use a cellular Apple Watch, and she doesn't care about video quality, so she chose US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, saving $100 over the Unlimited Premium plan I chose. Paying $500 for two lines plus an Apple Watch plan for a year is a much better deal than the $1,356 my wife and I paid T-Mobile for two lines for a year (without Apple Watch service). (To reiterate, this was already with the military discount!)

Getting a transfer PIN from T-Mobile was straightforward; I'd half-expected it to be buried and complicated. Here are instructions for Verizon and AT&T as well.

After my iPhone connected to Wi-Fi, US Mobile emailed me a new eSIM, and installation was as simple as tapping a button in the email and following the on-screen prompts. My wife's iPhone followed the same process. The only extra step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I did easily through US Mobile's app.

Why I'm Staying with an MVNO

Same coverage, lower bill: For the money I save, the compromises I've made are well worth it. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so my mobile data needs aren't that high (though in speed tests, US Mobile's speeds were just as fast as T-Mobile's). What matters most to me is having a strong, stable cellular signal when I'm off Wi-Fi, especially for making and receiving calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have already done away with traditional contract plans in favor of device installment plans, which effectively accomplish the same thing—keeping you on their network until you've paid off the device. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I want the freedom of an unlocked phone, but I like that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible all don't require contracts.

Easy to switch carriers: Most MVNOs let you pay month-to-month, so you're not locked into long-term contracts. If one carrier has a good deal one month and another has a better deal the next, switching is quick and easy. Prepaid accounts also don't require a credit check, meaning switching carriers won't impact your credit record with a hard inquiry, and you won't be denied service based on your credit history, unlike with postpaid accounts. My credit record isn't bad, but I didn't want a hard inquiry from switching from T-Mobile to Verizon to ding my credit score.

Top comment from Zach Chadwick

I've been with T-Mobile since 2014. Two lines came to $135 with Device Promotional Trade-in. After price hikes, new plan changes, and trade-in requirements, my monthly bill rose to $185.

I switched to Visible in September 2025. I went with their Pro plan and used the promo code SAVE26 for 26 months at $33 per month on their best plan.

After my mom's trade-in credit ran out, I switched her over too. At the time, they had a half-price annual deal on their best plan, so it was $275 for a year of service.

Our two lines cost us a combined $671 this year—that's just four months of my T-Mobile bill.

I haven't had any issues. I set up Autopay. They don't force you to use a debit card or checking account. I spend 90% of my time on 5G UW. I can also stream 4K seamlessly with no buffering.

I've also built a Visible "Circle" where I can invite others to join, and we get $5 back per line, which I use to help cover the bills for everyone in the circle.

Annual savings add up: There's a trade-off for flexibility—if you're willing to prepay for a year of service, you can usually save even more. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts for annual plans, so you're trading the freedom to switch at any time for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I love taking cruises. If you've ever forgotten to put your iPhone in airplane mode and ended up connecting to the ship's cellular network, you know you're likely in for a shocking bill. With a prepaid plan, I don't have to worry about accidentally racking up massive roaming charges. If roaming isn't included in the plan, my phone simply won't connect to a foreign network and charge me. US Mobile's plans also include taxes and fees, so the price is what you actually pay.

Switching to an MVNO isn't just about finding the cheapest service—it's about getting the service I want without paying for a bunch of stuff I don't want or need. So far, there's nothing I miss (though I know I'll definitely miss that free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I now have an extra Apple Watch line I didn't have before, but my monthly bill is still lower. I'm using the same iPhones, the same phone numbers, coverage in my area is better on US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network, and if I find a better option down the road, I still have the freedom to switch.

Your priorities may differ from mine, and an MVNO may not be the right choice for everyone. But if your wireless bill is high and you haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth a look. You might be surprised at how little you're actually giving up.
